task_description: Print the full path of the current working directory.

per_tile_feedback.pwd: Correct! pwd stands for 'print working directory' and displays the absolute path.
per_tile_feedback.ls: ls lists files and folders, not the current path.
per_tile_feedback.cd: cd changes the directory, it does not print the current location.
per_tile_feedback.dir: dir is a Windows command for listing directory contents, not for printing the working directory.

hints: Remember that the command is an acronym for 'print working directory'.
It is a three‑letter command, not related to listing files.
explanation: pwd outputs the absolute path of the current directory, helping you know exactly where you are in the filesystem.

task_description: List the files and directories in the current folder.

per_tile_feedback.ls: Correct! ls lists the contents of the current directory.
per_tile_feedback.pwd: pwd prints the working directory path, not its contents.
per_tile_feedback.list: list is not a valid shell command.
per_tile_feedback.show: show is not a standard command for listing files.

hints: This two‑letter command is short for 'list'.
It shows the names of files and subdirectories, not the path.
explanation: ls lists files and directories. By default it hides files whose names start with a dot; use ls -a to include them.

task_description: Change the current working directory to the folder named archive.

per_tile_feedback.cd: Correct! cd stands for 'change directory' and moves the shell into the archive folder.
per_tile_feedback.mv: mv is used to move or rename files, not to change the shell's working directory.
per_tile_feedback.chdir: chdir is a Windows command; on Unix-like systems the command is cd.
per_tile_feedback.goto: goto is not a shell command for changing directories.

hints: The command is two letters, an abbreviation of 'change directory'.
You use it to navigate into subdirectories.
explanation: cd archive moves the shell's current location into the archive folder. Without arguments, cd goes to the home directory.

task_description: Check the installed version of Git.

per_tile_feedback.--version: Correct! The double‑dash flag is the standard way to display the Git version.
per_tile_feedback.version: Without the dashes, 'git version' is not a recognized Git subcommand.
per_tile_feedback.-v: The -v flag is not used by Git for version information.
per_tile_feedback.--ver: The correct long flag is --version, not --ver.

hints: Many command‑line tools use --version to show their version number.
It requires two dashes before the word 'version'.
explanation: git --version prints the installed Git version, e.g., 'git version 2.46.0'. Using 'git version' without dashes is a common mistake.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Writing 'git version' without dashes will produce an error.

task_description: Create a new Git repository inside a directory named mental-health-workspace.

per_tile_feedback.mental-health-workspace: Correct! The argument is the name of the directory to create and initialize.
per_tile_feedback.my-project: This would create a repository named 'my-project', not the required 'mental-health-workspace'.
per_tile_feedback.repo: The name must match the exact project directory.
A dot initializes the current directory, not a new one.

hints: Use the exact name from the course: the project is about mental health in tech.
The directory will be created and a hidden .git folder placed inside it.
explanation: git init mental-health-workspace creates the folder and turns it into a Git repository.

task_description: Convert the current directory into a Git repository.

per_tile_feedback.init: Correct! git init without a directory name initializes the current folder.
per_tile_feedback.start: Git does not have a 'start' subcommand.
per_tile_feedback.repo: 'git repo' is not a valid command.

hints: The command is short for 'initialize'.
It creates the hidden .git folder in the current directory.
explanation: git init (without arguments) turns the present working directory into a Git repository by creating the .git subfolder.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Running git init inside an existing repository creates nested repos, causing confusion.

task_description: Check the current state of the repository to see which files are tracked, modified, or untracked.

per_tile_feedback.status: Correct! git status shows the working tree status and staging area.
per_tile_feedback.log: git log shows commit history, not the current file states.
per_tile_feedback.diff: git diff shows changes, but status gives an overview of all files.

hints: You run this frequently to see what's changed since the last commit.
It lists untracked files and files that are staged.
explanation: git status displays the current branch, changes to be committed, changes not staged, and untracked files.

task_description: Complete the hint that appears in git status output when untracked files are present.
code_template: nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to _____)

per_tile_feedback.track: Correct! The status message suggests using 'git add' to begin tracking the files.
per_tile_feedback.commit: Adding does not commit directly; it only stages.
per_tile_feedback.stage: The message specifically says 'to track', not 'to stage'.
per_tile_feedback.ignore: You would use .gitignore to ignore files, not 'git add'.

hints: The full message says: use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed, which is also called 'tracking'.
The blank is the action Git performs on previously untracked files when you run git add.
explanation: The status message reads 'nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)'.

task_description: Stage the file README.md for the next commit.

per_tile_feedback.README.md: Correct! Only this file will be staged.
The dot stages all files in the current directory, not just README.md.
per_tile_feedback.*: The wildcard * may not match hidden files and is less precise.
per_tile_feedback.add: You cannot write 'git add add' – the argument must be a file path.

hints: Use the exact filename from the course example.
The file is a Markdown readme.
explanation: git add README.md stages that single file, preparing its current contents for the next commit.

task_description: Stage all new and modified files in the current directory and its subdirectories.

Correct! The dot tells Git to stage everything from the current directory downwards, respecting .gitignore.
per_tile_feedback.*: The shell expands * before Git sees it, potentially missing dotfiles.
per_tile_feedback.--all: --all is not used with git add; it is a flag for git commit.
per_tile_feedback.-A: -A is not a valid short flag for git add.

hints: Think of the symbol that represents the current directory.
The course uses a single punctuation character for this.
explanation: git add . recursively adds all changes in the current directory and below, while ignoring files listed in .gitignore.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Using 'git add *' can behave differently because the shell expands the wildcard before Git processes it.

task_description: Commit the staged changes with the exact message 'Adding a README.'

Correct! The course example uses exactly this message.
per_tile_feedback.Add README: The message in the course is 'Adding a README.', not 'Add README'.
per_tile_feedback.Added README: The tense does not match the course example.
per_tile_feedback.Update readme: This does not describe the specific action performed.

hints: Look at the commit message in the code example from Chapter 3.
The message begins with 'Adding' and ends with a period.
explanation: git commit -m "Adding a README." creates a new snapshot with that log message, using the -m flag to supply the message inline.

task_description: Create a commit with the message 'Fix typos' without being dropped into a text editor.

per_tile_feedback.-m: Correct! The -m flag lets you provide the commit message directly on the command line.
per_tile_feedback.--msg: The correct long flag is --message, but the course uses the short -m.
per_tile_feedback.-a: -a automatically stages modified tracked files, but does not supply a message.
per_tile_feedback.-e: -e forces the editor to open even when -m is used; it does not help skip the editor.

hints: The flag is a single hyphen followed by a letter.
It stands for 'message'.
explanation: git commit -m "message" creates a commit with that message, bypassing the default text editor.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Omitting the -m flag will open the configured editor, which can confuse beginners.

task_description: Using the output of git log below, run a command to view the details of the commit that has the hash starting with ad8acfe.
code_template:
git log --oneline
ad8acfe Add README
cb33c18 Update data

git show _____

per_tile_feedback.ad8acfe: Correct! That is the shortened commit hash of the first entry, which identifies the commit.
per_tile_feedback.cb33c18: That hash belongs to the second commit, not the one you want to inspect.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD: HEAD would show the latest commit, which is cb33c18, not ad8acfe.
per_tile_feedback.main: main is a branch name, not a specific commit hash.

hints: Use the shortened hash from the log output, not a branch name.
The commit you want is the one with the message 'Add README'.
explanation: Git can reference commits by their unique hash. Even a short prefix like ad8acfe is enough to identify the commit, as long as it's unambiguous.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ The hash is deterministic and not random; the same content always produces the same hash.

task_description: Display the full commit history of the repository.

per_tile_feedback.log: Correct! git log shows the commit history in reverse chronological order.
per_tile_feedback.commits: 'git commits' is not a valid command.
per_tile_feedback.show: git show displays a single commit, not the whole history.

hints: The command is three letters.
It's the primary way to review past snapshots.
explanation: git log opens a pager (like less) that lists commits with their hashes, authors, dates, and messages. Press q to exit.

task_description: Complete the author name from a git log entry.
code_template:
commit ad8acfef94cb924444c488132bdef7c54b9bcac68
Author: _____ <repl@datacamp.com>
Date:   Wed Jul 24 07:48:27 2022 +0000

per_tile_feedback.Rep Loop: Correct! The course output consistently uses 'Rep Loop' as the author name.
per_tile_feedback.Repl User: The email domain is repl@datacamp.com, but the display name is 'Rep Loop'.
per_tile_feedback.DataCamp: This is the organisation, not the author name.
per_tile_feedback.Git User: This is a generic placeholder, not the actual author from the course example.

hints: The name appears in the git log output from Chapter 4.
It consists of two words, starting with 'Rep'.
explanation: The git log output shows the commit author. In the course examples, the author is consistently 'Rep Loop'.

task_description: Show only the three most recent commits.

per_tile_feedback.-3: Correct! The course uses the compact -<number> syntax.
per_tile_feedback.-n 3: This is also valid and means the same thing; both are accepted.
per_tile_feedback.--max 3: --max is not a recognized git log option.
per_tile_feedback.--last 3: --last is not a valid flag for git log.

hints: The flag is a hyphen directly followed by a number.
In Chapter 5, the example uses 'git log -3'.
explanation: git log -3 restricts the output to the three latest commits. The syntax -<n> is a shortcut.

task_description: List all commits made after April 2, 2024.

per_tile_feedback.Apr 2 2024: Correct! The course example uses this exact date format.
per_tile_feedback.April 2, 2024: The course format does not include a comma; this might still work but is not the exact example.
per_tile_feedback.2024-04-02: Git accepts this ISO format, so it's a valid alternative.
per_tile_feedback.2 Apr 2024: Git understands many date formats, but the course example is 'Apr 2 2024'.

hints: The course shows the date as 'Apr 2 2024' without a comma.
The month is abbreviated to three letters, followed by the day and year.
explanation: git log --since='Apr 2 2024' shows commits on or after that date. Git accepts various natural language formats.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Ambiguous formats like '07-04-2024' can be misinterpreted depending on locale.

task_description: Display commits made between April 2 and April 11, 2024.

per_tile_feedback.Apr 11 2024: Correct! This matches the course example for the end of the range.
per_tile_feedback.Apr 10 2024: The course example uses April 11, not April 10.
per_tile_feedback.2024-04-11: Git accepts this ISO format, so it's a valid alternative.
per_tile_feedback.11 Apr 2024: Git may understand this, but the exact course format is 'Apr 11 2024'.

hints: The course example uses the same format as --since.
The day is 11, not 10.
explanation: git log --until='Apr 11 2024' limits the history to commits up to that date. Combined with --since, it creates a date window.

task_description: See the unstaged changes made to report.md since the last commit.

per_tile_feedback.diff: Correct! git diff compares the working file to the version in the last commit.
per_tile_feedback.show: git show displays a commit, not working directory differences.
per_tile_feedback.status: git status reports which files have changed, not the actual line differences.

hints: The command stands for 'difference'.
It outputs lines prefixed with + and -.
explanation: git diff report.md shows the exact lines added and removed in the unstaged version of the file.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ git diff without --staged only shows unstaged changes.

task_description:
In the diff output below, what does the '+' indicate?

-TODO: write executive summary.
+TODO: cite funding sources.

per_tile_feedback.added: Correct! Lines with '+' are new additions.
per_tile_feedback.modified: A modification is shown as a removal of the old line and an addition of the new line.
per_tile_feedback.unchanged: Unchanged lines appear without a prefix in the context.

hints: Lines starting with '-' are deletions.
Lines starting with '+' are the opposite.
explanation: In unified diff output, '+' marks lines that have been added, while '-' marks lines that have been removed.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ A single modification is represented as a delete and an add pair.

task_description: Compare the staged version of report.md to the last commit.

per_tile_feedback.--staged: Correct! --staged shows the difference between the staging area and HEAD.
per_tile_feedback.--cached: This is a synonym for --staged and is also valid.
per_tile_feedback.--stage: --stage is not a recognized flag; the correct long form is --staged.
per_tile_feedback.-s: The short flag -s is not used for --staged.

hints: The flag begins with '--st' and tells Git to look at the staging area.
Without this flag, git diff only shows unstaged changes.
explanation: git diff --staged (or --cached) compares what is staged to the last commit, showing exactly what will be committed.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Forgetting the --staged flag will show no output if the changes have already been staged.

task_description: Compare the previous commit to the current commit using relative references.

per_tile_feedback.HEAD: Correct! HEAD is the current commit, while HEAD~1 is its parent.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD~0: HEAD~0 is not a valid reference; HEAD~1 is the parent.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD~2: That would compare two commits back to two commits back, not the current one.
per_tile_feedback.main: main is a branch name, not a relative reference to the current commit.

hints: HEAD without a tilde points to where you currently are.
The command should show the difference between the parent and the current commit.
explanation: git diff HEAD~1 HEAD shows what changed between the previous commit and the latest one.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Order matters: git diff HEAD HEAD~1 would show the reverse of the changes.

task_description: View the full details (metadata and patch) of the commit identified by the hash c27fa856.

per_tile_feedback.show: Correct! git show displays the commit object and its diff.
per_tile_feedback.log: git log shows the entire history, not a single commit.
per_tile_feedback.diff: git diff compares two commits, but a single hash doesn't provide the other commit.

hints: You need to inspect one specific commit, not the whole history.
The command is four letters.
explanation: git show <commit> presents the metadata (author, date, message) and the changes introduced by that commit.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Confusing git show with git log or git diff is a common mistake.

task_description: Undo the most recent commit by creating a new commit that reverses its changes.

per_tile_feedback.revert: Correct! git revert creates a new commit that inverts the target commit's changes.
per_tile_feedback.reset: git reset can discard commits, but it rewrites history and does not create a new safe commit.
per_tile_feedback.checkout: git checkout can switch branches or restore files, but it does not create a revert commit.

hints: The command starts with 'rev' and preserves the original commit in history.
It's the safe way to undo a public commit.
explanation: git revert HEAD computes the inverse of the latest commit and records it as a new commit, leaving all history intact.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ git revert does not delete the original commit; it adds a new one.

task_description: Revert the commit with the hash 35f4b4d.

per_tile_feedback.35f4b4d: Correct! The hash from the course identifies the commit to revert.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD: HEAD would revert the latest commit, not the specific one with that hash.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD~1: That refers to the parent commit, not 35f4b4d.
per_tile_feedback.main: main is a branch, not a commit hash.

hints: Use the exact hash shown in the task description.
It's a 7-character hexadecimal string.
explanation: git revert <commit> creates a new commit that undoes the changes from that commit. You can reference it by its full or abbreviated hash.

task_description: Revert the latest commit without being prompted to edit the commit message.

per_tile_feedback.HEAD: Correct! HEAD refers to the most recent commit.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD~1: That would revert the parent commit, not the latest.
per_tile_feedback.main: main is a branch name, but HEAD already points to the latest commit on the current branch.
A dot is not a valid commit reference.

hints: You need to reference the latest commit.
The symbolic reference that means 'current commit'.
explanation: git revert --no-edit HEAD creates a revert commit for HEAD using the default revert message, skipping the editor.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Using --no-edit when you want to customize the message is a common oversight.

task_description: Apply the inverse of the latest commit's changes to the working directory and staging area, but do not create a commit.

per_tile_feedback.HEAD: Correct! The -n flag applies the revert changes without committing.
per_tile_feedback.HEAD~1: This would target the parent commit, not the latest.
per_tile_feedback.main: main is a branch name; HEAD is already pointing to it.
A dot is not a commit reference.

hints: -n stands for '--no-commit'.
You need to specify which commit to revert; the current commit is the target.
explanation: git revert -n HEAD stages the reverse of the latest commit but stops before creating a commit, allowing review or combination with other changes.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Forgetting to follow up with a commit leaves the revert changes staged but unsaved.

task_description: Restore the file report.md to its state from the previous commit.

per_tile_feedback.report.md: Correct! This is the file we want to restore.
per_tile_feedback.README.md: The task specifies report.md, not README.md.
per_tile_feedback.summary_statistics.csv: This is a different file from the course examples.
A dot would try to restore a directory, not a single file.

hints: Use the exact filename from the task description.
The double dash -- separates the commit reference from the file path.
explanation: git checkout <commit> -- <file> overwrites the working copy of the file with the version from that commit.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Forgetting the -- separator can cause Git to misinterpret the file name as a branch name.

task_description: Remove summary_statistics.csv from the staging area but keep its changes in the working directory.

per_tile_feedback.restore: Correct! git restore --staged unstages the file.
per_tile_feedback.reset: git reset can also unstage files, but the course teaches git restore --staged as the modern method.
per_tile_feedback.unstage: Git does not have an 'unstage' subcommand.

hints: The command starts with 'res' and is the newer way to unstage files.
It is used with the --staged flag to target the staging area.
explanation: git restore --staged <file> moves a file out of the staging area, leaving the working directory unchanged.
common_mistake_warning: ⚠️ Without --staged, git restore would discard your working changes entirely.

task_description: Unstage only the file summary_statistics.csv using the restore command.

per_tile_feedback.summary_statistics.csv: Correct! This is the file to unstage.
A dot would unstage all files, not just the specified one.
per_tile_feedback.--all: This is not a valid file path; you need the filename.

hints: Use the exact filename from the task.
The command ends with the file you want to unstage.
explanation: git restore --staged summary_statistics.csv removes that specific file from the staging area, so it will not be included in the next commit.
